body_es: Test-Driven Development sigue el ciclo Red-Green-Refactor: primero se escribe un test que falla porque la función aún no existe (rojo), luego se escribe el código mínimo necesario para que pase (verde), y por último se mejora la implementación sin cambiar su comportamiento observable (refactor), apoyándose en el test para detectar cualquier ruptura. Behavior-Driven Development extiende esta idea describiendo el comportamiento en pasos legibles por el negocio —"dado", "cuando", "entonces"— que se traducen a llamadas de código concretas, de modo que un product manager puede leer el escenario y entender qué se está probando sin leer Python. Por ejemplo, una función `validate_password` puede empezar solo comprobando la longitud mínima (para pasar un test con contraseñas cortas y largas), y luego añadir en el paso de refactor comprobaciones de mayúscula y dígito porque el test original ya cubría esos casos como fallidos. El error habitual es escribir el test después del código en lugar de antes: entonces el test tiende a confirmar lo que el código ya hace, incluidos sus bugs, en vez de definir de forma independiente qué comportamiento es correcto.
body_en: Test-Driven Development follows the Red-Green-Refactor cycle: first a test is written that fails because the function doesn't exist yet (red), then the minimal code needed to make it pass is written (green), and finally the implementation is improved without changing its observable behavior (refactor), relying on the test to catch any regression along the way. Behavior-Driven Development extends this idea by describing behavior in business-readable steps —"given", "when", "then"— that translate into concrete code calls, so a product manager or a QA analyst can read the scenario and understand what's being tested without reading Python. For example, a `validate_password` function can start by only checking minimum length (to pass a test with short and long passwords), then gain uppercase and digit checks in the refactor step because the original test already covered those cases as failing. The common mistake is writing the test after the code instead of before: then the test tends to confirm whatever the code already does, bugs included, instead of independently defining what correct behavior actually looks like.
example_code:
import re


# GREEN: minimal implementation written after the test below was red
def validate_password(password):
    if len(password) < 8:
        return False
    if not re.search(r"[A-Z]", password):
        return False
    if not re.search(r"[0-9]", password):
        return False
    return True


# The test written first (TDD), now passing against the implementation above
def test_password_validation():
    cases = [
        ("weak", False),
        ("nouppercase1", False),
        ("StrongPass123", True),
    ]
    for password, expected in cases:
        assert validate_password(password) == expected, password
    return len(cases)


# BDD scenario expressed as plain steps, driving the same function
def bdd_scenario_user_registers(email, password):
    given_page_open = True
    when_email_filled = given_page_open and "@" in email
    when_password_filled = when_email_filled and validate_password(password)
    then_registered = when_password_filled
    return then_registered


passed = test_password_validation()
print(f"test_password_validation PASSED ({passed} cases)")

scenario_ok = bdd_scenario_user_registers("user@example.com", "SecurePass123")
print(f"Scenario: user registers with valid credentials -> {'PASSED' if scenario_ok else 'FAILED'}")

scenario_bad = bdd_scenario_user_registers("user@example.com", "weak")
print(f"Scenario: user registers with weak password -> {'PASSED' if not scenario_bad else 'FAILED'}")
example_output:
test_password_validation PASSED (3 cases)
Scenario: user registers with valid credentials -> PASSED
Scenario: user registers with weak password -> PASSED
